title: Speculative Execution Attacks: Spectre and Meltdown

sections.heading: Speculative Execution: Why CPUs Guess
sections.body:
A modern out-of-order core splits work between an instruction control unit, which fetches and decodes far ahead of where the program is actually executing, and an execution unit, which retires results once it is sure they are correct. The gap between the two exists because a conditional branch cannot be resolved until its condition is computed, yet the fetch unit must keep issuing work every cycle to keep the execution unit busy. The fix is branch prediction: guess taken/not-taken and the target address, then begin fetching, decoding and even executing instructions along the guessed path before the branch actually resolves — this is speculative execution. If the guess was right, the work already done is retired for free. If it was wrong, the processor discards every register and memory effect computed along the wrong path and resumes fetching at the correct target, exactly as if the wrong-path instructions had never run.

This squash-and-restart behaviour is not exotic; it happens on every mispredicted branch, all the time. A typical CPI decomposition for a simple pipelined design puts a number on it: if a fraction of instructions are conditional jumps, only some of those are mispredicted, and each misprediction injects a fixed number of bubbles, the misprediction penalty is their product. With 20% of instructions being conditional jumps, 40% of those mispredicted, and 2 bubbles per misprediction, the penalty term is $0.20 \times 0.40 \times 2 = 0.16$ cycles per instruction — a real but modest cost added to a base CPI of 1. The architectural contract is airtight: whatever the predictor guesses, the program's registers and memory end up exactly as sequential execution would have left them. Spectre and Meltdown exploit the one thing that contract says nothing about: the cache.

sections.heading: The Side Channel: Cache State Outlives the Squash
sections.body:
When a misprediction is discovered, the reorder buffer discards every in-flight instruction's register and memory writes. It does not, and cannot cheaply, undo whatever those instructions did to shared microarchitectural structures — the data cache, the TLB, the branch predictor's own tables. A load executed on a path that turns out to be wrong still pulls its cache line into L1 and leaves it there. That line's continued presence is not an architectural side effect (no register holds it, no memory location changed), but it is measurable, because a cache hit and a cache miss take different amounts of time.

Flush+Reload (Yarom & Falkner, 2014) turns that timing gap into a channel. The attacker shares a physical page with the victim (a mapped shared library page, for example), and for a chosen cache line: (1) evicts it with `clflush`; (2) waits while the victim, or a squashed speculative path, runs; (3) times a reload of the same address. A fast reload means someone touched that line during the wait; a slow one means nobody did. The Core i7 hierarchy used in the course slides makes the gap concrete: an L1 hit costs about 4 cycles, an L2 hit about 11, and a shared L3 hit 30-40 cycles, while a genuine miss has to go all the way to DRAM, at latency far beyond any of those. A single timed access reliably tells hit from miss because the two cases are separated by roughly an order of magnitude, not by noise-level differences — which is exactly why one `clflush`/access/reload triple is enough to extract one bit (or, against 256 candidate lines, one byte) of secret-dependent state, all without ever violating a single architectural guarantee.

sections.heading: Meltdown: Racing the Permission Check
sections.body:
Meltdown (Lipp et al., 2018; CVE-2017-5754) attacks a narrower, CPU-specific bug: on the affected out-of-order designs, a load's data can come back from the cache and be used by dependent instructions *before* the MMU's privilege check on that load has been resolved. If the address is kernel-only and the code is running in user mode, the load will eventually fault — but by the time it does, a dependent instruction may already have used the illegally-read byte to index a probe array, changing which of its cache lines is resident. The fault is then delivered and the whole speculative sequence is architecturally discarded, exactly like an ordinary misprediction — except the cache-residency side effect survives, and Flush+Reload against the probe array recovers the byte.

The reason this could read *kernel* memory specifically is a software decision, not a hardware one: for speed, the kernel's entire address range was mapped into every process's page tables (just marked supervisor-only), so that switching from user to kernel mode on a syscall or interrupt did not require reloading the page-table base register or flushing the TLB. That mapping being present — merely permission-denied — is exactly what a speculative load can race past. Kernel Page-Table Isolation (KPTI) fixes this by giving each process two page tables: a full one, used only while executing kernel code, and a minimal user-mode one that maps just a small trampoline needed to handle the next syscall or interrupt, with no exploitable kernel data left to race against. The cost is an extra page-table (CR3) reload, and the TLB pressure that comes with it, on every kernel entry and exit; workloads dominated by syscalls or interrupts feel this far more than CPU-bound code that rarely crosses the boundary. Note what KPTI does *not* do: it does not touch branch prediction or speculative execution at all, so it has no effect whatsoever on Spectre.

sections.heading: Spectre v1: Bounds-Check Bypass
sections.body:
Spectre v1 (Kocher et al., 2018; CVE-2017-5753) targets the most ordinary defensive pattern in systems code: a bounds check before an array access, of exactly the shape the course material shows for `combine4b`'s `if (i >= 0 && i < v->len)` guard. Such a branch is overwhelmingly predictable — true on almost every call — which is precisely why the hardware predicts it, runs ahead of it, and only checks its work afterwards. Spectre v1 abuses that predictability directly: an attacker calls a victim function many times with legitimate, in-bounds indices, training the branch predictor to expect 'condition true, proceed.' It then calls the same function once with an out-of-bounds index. Architecturally nothing unsafe happens — the comparison still correctly evaluates to false and the guarded body never executes in the program's sequential semantics. But the mistrained predictor speculatively executes the guarded body anyway, before the comparison resolves: it loads the out-of-bounds byte and uses it, scaled by a stride wide enough to land on its own cache line (so that 256 possible byte values map to 256 distinguishable lines), to index a second array. That touch is squashed once the branch resolves — but the cache-line residency it left behind is not, and Flush+Reload against the 256 candidates reads off the out-of-bounds byte.

The mechanism this relies on is not hypothetical inside CENG331 material either: the branch-through-a-loop example in the course slides shows the predictor guessing 'taken' through a vector of length 100 and, on the mispredicted final iteration, fetching and executing a read at the invalid index 101 before the misprediction is caught. Spectre v1 is that same predict-past-the-end behaviour, deliberately induced on a chosen index rather than encountered by accident on a loop's last iteration, with the byte it reads made observable through cache timing instead of being silently discarded. The accompanying code listing is a faithful skeleton of the victim function and the mistraining loop; run without a genuine timing side channel it is completely safe, since the bounds check always fires architecturally — the vulnerability lives entirely in what the hardware does *before* that check is confirmed.

sections.heading: Mitigations and Trade-offs
sections.body:
Because Meltdown and Spectre are different bugs, they need different fixes, and neither one covers the other. Meltdown is closed by KPTI (software) or by hardware that resolves the permission check before the load can be used (later Intel and AMD silicon). Spectre v1's conditional-branch bypass is closed per dangerous site, not globally: a serializing instruction (`lfence`) after the bounds check blocks speculation past it entirely, and index masking (`idx &= (array1_size - 1)` for a power-of-two size) makes any speculative access land back in bounds instead of removing speculation. Neither is applied to every bounds check in a program, because branch prediction and speculation are exactly what keep a pipelined, multi-issue execution unit fed — the course material's own optimization and processor-design slides are built around exploiting that ILP, and serializing every guarded array access would give a lot of it back.

Spectre v2 (branch target injection, CVE-2017-5715) is a separate variant: instead of mistraining a conditional branch, the attacker poisons the CPU's indirect-branch predictor (used for virtual calls, switch-based jump tables, and PLT stubs) so a victim's indirect branch speculatively jumps to an attacker-chosen gadget address. The standard mitigation is the retpoline: the compiler replaces an indirect call or jump with a sequence that pushes the real target on the stack and returns to it, while priming the return-stack predictor to land on an infinite-loop trap if it is ever influenced by outside code. This costs an extra call/return pair per indirect branch — noticeable on code with many megamorphic call sites, negligible on ordinary direct calls — but needs no help from the OS or the hardware. Later CPU generations added hardware indirect-branch restriction as a cheaper, always-on alternative, reducing how much of this cost has to be paid in software as older, more exposed hardware is retired.

code.caption: Spectre v1 victim function and mistraining loop (after Kocher et al., 2018): architecturally the bounds check always fires, so this runs safely with no real cache-timing measurement attached.

worked_example.problem: The Core i7 hierarchy from the course slides [excerpt 4] gives L1 (32 KB, 8-way, 64 B lines), L2 (256 KB, 8-way, 64 B lines) and L3 (8 MB, 16-way, 64 B lines). Using $C = S \times E \times B$, find the number of sets $S$ and the number of set-index bits for each level. Then explain why an attacker without `clflush` — sandboxed JavaScript in a browser, for instance, which is exactly the setting the original Spectre proof of concept targeted — needs this arithmetic to mount Prime+Probe instead of Flush+Reload, and how many addresses are needed to build one eviction set for L2.
worked_example.solution:
From $C = S \times E \times B$, $S = C / (E \times B)$.

**L1:** $S = 32768 / (8 \times 64) = 64 = 2^6$, so 6 set-index bits (and, with $B=64=2^6$, 6 block-offset bits).

**L2:** $S = 262144 / (8 \times 64) = 512 = 2^9$, so 9 set-index bits.

**L3:** $S = 8388608 / (16 \times 64) = 8192 = 2^{13}$, so 13 set-index bits.

Flush+Reload needs `clflush` and a physical page shared with the victim — unavailable to code running inside a JavaScript sandbox, which has no cache-management instructions and no shared memory with the process it is attacking. Prime+Probe replaces eviction-by-instruction with eviction-by-contention: fill an entire cache set with the attacker's own addresses ("prime"), let the victim run, then time a reload of each of those same addresses ("probe") — any address now slow to reload was evicted by something the victim touched. Building a priming set for one set of the 8-way L2 therefore needs addresses whose low 9 set-index bits match and whose tags differ, and — because L2 is 8-way — at least $E = 8$ such addresses to fill every line of that set; real implementations collect a few more than 8 to compensate for non-LRU replacement policies. There are $2^9 = 512$ such sets to search over for L2, and correspondingly $2^6 = 64$ for L1 and $2^{13} = 8192$ for L3 — the same $(t, s, b)$ address breakdown the course cache slides use for an ordinary cache read is exactly the information a Prime+Probe attacker needs to target one specific set.

pitfalls: Assuming a security bug needs an architectural (ISA-visible) side effect. Spectre and Meltdown show that a purely microarchitectural one — which cache line is resident — is enough, because timing makes it observable.

Believing a correct bounds check (`if (i >= 0 && i < v->len)`, exactly the CS:APP `combine4b` pattern) makes an array access safe. It is safe architecturally; it says nothing about what the hardware executes before the check resolves.

Conflating Meltdown and Spectre. Meltdown is a specific out-of-order/permission-check ordering bug, largely fixed by KPTI plus later hardware; Spectre is a broad class present on essentially any predicting, speculating CPU, with a different mitigation per variant.
Assuming retpoline is a general Spectre fix. It only protects indirect branches against branch-target injection (v2); it does nothing for a mistrained conditional branch's bounds-check bypass (v1).

Assuming KPTI is free. It adds a page-table (CR3) reload and TLB refill on every kernel entry and exit, so syscall- and interrupt-heavy workloads pay noticeably more than CPU-bound code that rarely traps.

Thinking disabling compiler optimizations or loop unrolling helps. The vulnerable behaviour lives in the branch predictor and the cache, not in any particular compiler transformation, so it survives at -O0.
applications: Linux, Windows and macOS all shipped Kernel Page-Table Isolation (or an equivalent, KVA shadowing on Windows) within weeks of the January 2018 disclosure specifically to blunt Meltdown on affected CPUs.

Browser vendors (Chrome, Firefox) reduced JavaScript timer resolution and shipped site isolation (process-per-origin) because the original Spectre proof of concept showed sandboxed JS could read its host process's memory via cache timing alone.

GCC, Clang/LLVM and MSVC added retpoline code-generation flags (`-mindirect-branch=thunk`, `/Qspectre`) so existing C/C++ codebases could be rebuilt without hand-editing every indirect call or virtual dispatch site.

Multi-tenant cloud hypervisors (Xen, KVM) added indirect-branch-prediction barriers on VM-exit and vCPU context switch, since without them one tenant's speculative gadget training could target another tenant sharing the same physical core.

CPU vendors redesigned later microarchitectures (enhanced/always-on indirect-branch restriction, reworked permission-check ordering) to move these mitigations into hardware and reduce the software overhead paid by every kernel entry and every indirect call.

self_check.question: Why does a mispredicted branch normally cost only a handful of pipeline bubbles and nothing else, while a mistrained branch feeding a Spectre v1 gadget leaks a secret byte? What exactly is different about the two cases?
self_check.answer: Nothing is different about the branch mechanism itself — both are ordinary speculative execution followed by a squash when the misprediction is discovered. The difference is what the wrong-path instructions touch. An ordinary mispredicted branch in typical code executes instructions whose only externally-visible effect would have been registers and memory, both of which the reorder buffer discards perfectly on a squash — so nothing observable survives. A Spectre v1 gadget's wrong-path instructions include a load whose *address* depends on secret data, and that load changes which cache line is resident — a side effect the squash does not undo. The leak isn't a special kind of misprediction; it's an ordinary misprediction whose collateral damage happens to be readable with a clock.

self_check.question: An attacker wants to Prime+Probe one set of the L1 data cache described in the course slides (32 KB, 8-way associative, 64-byte lines) without using `clflush`. How many distinct addresses must map to that same set to fill it, and how many different sets does the attacker have to be able to target across the whole cache?
self_check.answer: $S = C/(E \times B) = 32768/(8 \times 64) = 64$ sets, so 6 bits identify the set. Filling one 8-way set requires at least $E = 8$ addresses whose set-index bits agree and whose tags differ (in practice a few more, to survive a non-LRU replacement policy); an attacker who wants to cover the whole L1 needs eviction sets for all $64$ possible set-index values.

self_check.question: A colleague proposes fixing Spectre v1 once and for all by having the compiler insert an `lfence` after every array bounds check in the codebase. What does this buy, what does it cost, and why is it not what production compilers do by default?
self_check.answer: An `lfence` is a serializing instruction: it stops any later instruction from executing until everything before it, including the branch it follows, has fully resolved. Placed right after a bounds check, it closes the exact gap Spectre v1 needs, because the guarded body can no longer run speculatively before the check is confirmed. The cost is that bounds checks are extremely common — every safe array access in defensively-written C, and every array access in a memory-safe language's generated code — and each one becomes a pipeline stall instead of work the execution unit can overlap with everything else in flight. Given how much of a pipelined, multi-issue core's throughput comes from exactly that overlap, a blanket `lfence` would erase most of the benefit branch prediction exists to provide. Production toolchains instead apply it (or index masking, which costs nothing on the fast path) only at sites shown to be reachable by attacker-influenced data, such as kernel syscall-argument validation.

key_points: Squashing a mispredicted branch undoes registers and memory, but not cache-line residency.
Flush+reload: flush a line, wait, time a reload — fast means it was touched, slow means it wasn't.
Meltdown races a load's data against its own permission check; KPTI removes the kernel mapping it needs.
Spectre v1 mistrains a correct bounds check so its body runs speculatively for an out-of-range index.
Retpolines stop Spectre v2's indirect-branch injection; they do nothing for v1's conditional branches.
Mitigations are applied per dangerous site (lfence, index masking), not globally — speculation is the point.
tagline: Mistrain a predictor, let a bounds check run speculatively, then read the secret off which cache line got warm.
tldr: Speculative execution lets a CPU guess a branch outcome and run ahead of it, discarding registers and memory perfectly if the guess was wrong — but leaving cache-line residency behind, which is exactly the channel Meltdown and Spectre read from. Meltdown races a kernel-memory load against its own permission check and is closed by KPTI; Spectre v1 mistrains a correct bounds check into running its body speculatively on an attacker-chosen out-of-range index, closed only per-site with barriers or index masking; Spectre v2 poisons the indirect-branch predictor and is closed with retpolines. All three read out their result with a cache-timing side channel such as flush+reload.
